text.p: Singapore's exports, lifeblood of a vibrant economy, dropped more sharply than expected in August and leading economists said on Friday it could be six months before a full recovery.
Total exports fell 4.4 percent year-on-year after a 6.7 rise in July, the Trade Development Board (TDB) said.
It said non-oil domestic exports fell 6.3 percent to Singapore $7.01 billion (US$5 billion) in August in nomimal terms year-on-year after rising 6.3 percent in July.
The drop in non-oil domestic exports was worse than even the most pessimistic forecast.

Eight economist polled by Reuters earlier in the week had predicted an average year-on-year fall of 0.8 percent for August. The actual forecasts had ranged from a rise of 3.5 percent to a fall of 4.5 percent.

"The figures were clearly below market expectations," said Ng Bok Eng, regional economist at Deustsche Morgan Grenfell. "Those who have called for a recovery in the fourth quarter or even in the first quarter of 1997 might be too early."

"I think we are probably close to the bottom of the cycle now, even though any kind of meaningful recovery will probably not be seen until the second quarter of next year," said Liew Yin Sze, economist at brokerage J.M. Sassoon.
The TDB blamed the fall in exports on the slowdown in global demand for electronics and related products as well as an oversupply of semiconductors.
Electronics account for almost half Singapore's total industrial output and around 60 percent of non-oil exports.
"The slowdown was reflected in our key markets, mainly U.S., EU (European Union), Malaysia, Japan and Hong Kong," the TDB said.
Eddie Lee, regional economist at Vickers Ballas, said the greater than expected decline in exports pointed to a basic problem in the rapidly-evolving electronics industry.
By the time something is made it may be out of date and hard to sell, leaving manufacturers with stocks they have to figure out what to do with.
Lee said he expected the third quarter to be the weakest of the year, though when a recovery might take place was open for debate.
"It is a question of timing. In this industry, the turnaround can be very quick when it comes. I still expect a slight pick up by Christmas but manufacturers will remain very cautious."
Lee also said the electronics slowdown was cyclical and not structural. "Global computer demand is still on a structural uptrend with penetration levels very low outside of the U.S."
And despite the slowdown, there is no shortage of foreign investors willing to put their money into Singapore.
Foreign investment commiments for the first half total S$3.8 billion and should meet the government's full year target of S$8 billion, up from last year's S$6.8 nillion, Lee said.
